questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Which of the following transitions of $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ ion will give rise to spectral line which has same wavelength as the spectral line in hydrogen atom?
questions.solution:
Let the transition of electron in hydrogen atom $(Z=1)$ gives wavelength $\lambda_1$ for transition from $n_2 to n_1$, then
$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R Z^2 \left(\frac{1}{m^2}-\frac{1}{n^2}\right)
Here, $\lambda=\lambda_1, Z=1, m=n_1, n=n_2 $\frac{1}{\lambda_1}=$ R(1)^2 $\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)=R\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)$
Now, if electron makes transition in $\mathrm{He}^{+}$ ion from $n_4 to n_3$ and gives wavelength $\lambda_2$, then
$\begin{aligned}
\frac{1}{\lambda_2} & =R(2)^2\left(\frac{1}{n_3^2}-\frac{1}{n_4^4}\right) \\
& =R\left[\frac{1}{\left(\frac{n_3}{2}\right)^2}-\frac{1}{\left(\frac{n_4}{2}\right)^2}\right]
\end{aligned}$
Given that, $\quad \lambda_1=\lambda_2\Rightarrow R\left(\frac{1}{n_1^2}-\frac{1}{n_2^2}\right)=R   $\$left[\frac{1}{ \left(\frac{n_3}{2}\rright)^2}-\f frac{1}{\left(\frac{n_4}{2}\right)^2}\right]On comparing beth sides, we get
$n_1=$\frac{n_3}{2} \text{$ and }}n_2=$\frac{n_4}{2}$ The value of $ n_1, n_2, n_3 and n_4$ must be an integer, as they denote principal quantum number.
If $n_3=2 and n_4=4$, then the given condition is satisfied.$

$E_n=\frac{-13.6 e V}{n^2}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The angular momentum for the electron in Bohr's orbit is L. If the electron is assumed to revolve in second orbit of hydrogen atom, then the change in angular momentum will be:
questions.solution:
From the Bohr's quantization rule
Angular momentum $\mathrm{L}=\frac{\mathrm{nh}}{2 \pi}, \mathrm{L}_1=\frac{1. \mathrm{h}}{2 \pi}=\mathrm{L}$ (n=1$ for first orbit)
in (n=2$ for second orbit) $L_2=\frac{2 h}{2 \pi}=2 L$
Hence, change in angular momentum $\mathrm{L}_2-\mathrm{L}_1=2 \mathrm{ L}-\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{L}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A $12.5 \mathrm{eV}$ electron beam is used to bombard gaseous hydrogen at room temperature. The number of spectral lines emitted will be:
questions.solution:
If we assume electron in hydrogen atom takes energy $12.09 \mathrm{eV}$ from the incoming radiation, the maximum excited state of electron will be $n=3$. So, number of spectral lines is $\frac{3(3-1)}{2}=3$.
Here we assume some part of energy $12.5 \mathrm{eV}-12.09 \mathrm{eV}=0.41 \mathrm{eV}$ get lost due to collision.

questions.q: The stopping potential $\left(V_0\right)$ versus frequency $(v)$ of a graph for photoelectric effect in a metal. From the graph, the planck's constant $(h)$ is.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned} e V_0=h\left( v-v_0\right) & =h v-h v_0 \\ V_0 & =\left(\frac{h}{e}\right) v-\left(\frac{h}{e}\right) v_0 \quad \quad \ldots (i) \end{aligned}$ From $Eq. (i), it follows that the slope of the graph is \frac{h}{e}$. Therefore, $\begin{aligned} h=e \times \text{ slope }& =1.6 \times10^{-19} \times \frac{165-0}{(8-4) \times 10^{15}}\\ & =\frac{1.6 \times 10^{-19} \times 16.5}{4 \times 10^{15}}=6.6 \times10^{-34} \mathrm{ J}-\mathrm{s} . \end{aligned}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: $12$ eV energy is given to electron in third orbit of $H$-atom, then final energy of electron when it ionise from third orbit, is
questions.solution:
Given, total energy given to electron in third orbit,

$E = 12eV$

Energy of third orbit of $H$-atom, $E ' = \dfrac{- 13. 6}{n2}$

$= \dfrac{- 13. 6}{32} = - 1. 51eV$

lonisation energy of electron of third orbit, $E^{' '} = - E '$

$= - \left(- 1. 51eV\right) ⇒ E^{' '} = 1. 51eV$

Hence, final energy of electron when it comes out of $H$-atom from third orbit

${E}_{f} = E - E^{' '}$

$= 12 - 1. 51 = 10. 49eV$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The total energy of an electron in the first excited state of hydrogen is about $- 3. 4eV$. Its kinetic energy in this state is&
questions.solution:
We have, Kinetic energy of electron,

$K = \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{8\pi{ε}_{0} \cdot r}$

also, Potential energy of electron,

$U = - \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}} \cdot \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{r}$

$∴$ Total energy

$E = K + U$

$= \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{8\pi{ε}_{0} \cdot r} - \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{4\pi{ε}_{0} \cdot r}$

$E = - \dfrac{Ze^{2}}{8\pi{ε}_{0}r}$ or $K = - E = - \left(-3. 4\right)$

$= 3. 4eV

$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Monochromatic radiation of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident on a hydrogen sample in ground state. Hydrogen atom absorbs a fraction of light and subsequently emits radiations of six different wavelengths. The wavelength $\lambda$ is
questions.solution:
As $H$-atom emits $6$ spectral lines $\dfrac{n\left(n - 1\right)}{2} = 6$

$∴ n = 4$

$\Delta E = {E}_{4} - {E}_{1} = 13. 6 - 0. 85$

$= 12. 75eV$

$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{∆ E} = \dfrac{1242nm}{12. 75}$

$∴ \lambda = 97. 5nm$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: If the series limit wavelength of Lyman series for the hydrogen atom is $912 Å,$ then the series limit wavelength for Balmer series of hydrogen atoms is
questions.solution:
$\frac{1}{\lambda}=R\left[\frac{1}{n_{1}^{2}}-\frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right]$

For limiting wavelength of Lyman series

$$

n_{1}=1, n_{2}=\infty \quad \frac{1}{\lambda_{L}}=R

$$

For limiting wavelength of Balmer series $n_{1}=2, n_{2}=\infty$

$$

\begin{array}{l}

\frac{1}{\lambda_{B}}=R\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \Rightarrow \lambda_{B}=\frac{4}{R} \\

\therefore \lambda_{B}=4 \lambda_{L}=4 \times 912 \AA

\end{array}

$$

The electronic transition corresponding to this line is $\mathrm{n}=12 \rightarrow \mathrm{n}=\mathrm{x}.$ Find the value of $\mathrm{x}$
questions.solution: For $2^{\text{nd line$ of Balmer series in hydrogen }} spectrum $\frac{1}{\lambda}=\mathrm{R}(1)\left(\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{4^{2}}\right)=\frac{3}{16} \mathrm{R} \text{ For } \mathrm{Li}^{2+}\left[\frac{1}{\lambda}=\mathrm{R} \times9\left(\frac{1}{\mathrm{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{12^{2}}\right)=\frac{3 \mathrm{R}}{16}\right]$ which is satisfied by $n=12 \rightarrow n=6 $

questions.q: If hydrogen atom, an electron jumps from bigger orbit to smaller orbit so that radius of smaller orbit is one-fourth of radius of bigger orbit. If speed of electron in bigger orbit was $\mathrm{v}$, then speed in smaller orbit is
questions.solution: Radius of the orbit, $\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{n}} \propto \mathrm{n}^{2} \begin{aligned}& \frac{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{nbig}}}{\mathrm{r}_{\mathrm{n} \text{ small }}}=\frac{\mathrm{n}_{\text{big }^{2}}{\mathrm{n}_{\text{small }^{2}}=\frac{4}{1}\\ \Rightarrow & \frac{\mathrm{n}_{\text{big }}}{\mathrm{n}_{\text{small }}}=2 \\ \Rightarrow \text{ and } \frac{\mathrm{n}_{\text{small }}}{\mathrm{n}_{\text{big }}}=\frac{1}{2} \end{aligned}$ Velocity of electron in $\mathrm{n}^{\text{th }}$ orbit $\begin{array}{c} \quad\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n}} \propto \frac{1}{\mathrm{n}}\\ \frac{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n} \mathrm{big}}}{\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n} \text{ small }}}=\frac{\mathrm{n}_{\text{small }}}{\mathrm{n}_{\text{big }}}=\frac{1}{2}\\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n} \text{ small }}=2\left(\mathrm{v}_{\mathrm{n} \mathrm{big}}\right)=2 \mathrm{v} \end{array}$
